storm.summary_layperson: No storms anywhere near the area tonight — clear, cool, and calm, with the only weather note being a minor coastal flooding statement for tomorrow's high tide.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer at all: the Sound (60°F) is already warmer than the air at 4 PM, and the gap widens to ~7°F the other way by 8 PM as the air cools — moot tonight with no storms around.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: High pressure (about 1028 hPa) is in charge. KOKX radar shows no echoes to track, the model shows zero instability (CAPE 0 J/kg), and there are no watches or warnings. Upper-level wind shear is strong at about 49 kt from the WNW, but with no instability there is nothing for that shear to organize — it is a dry, stable fall evening.

Local modifier: None in play. The Sound's usual protective trick needs the water to be noticeably colder than the air (about 5°F or more) so a cool, stable layer sits over the water and starves storms. Tonight it is the reverse: Sound water is 60°F and the air is about 59°F at 4 PM. The air keeps cooling after the 5:56 PM sunset while the water holds steady, so by 8 PM the air is roughly 7°F colder than the water — no stable layer at any point in the window.

Most likely outcome for the cove: Same as everywhere else around — dry, clear, and quiet. No difference expected between the cove and inland towns.

One thing to note: NWS Upton has a Coastal Flood Statement (minor) for the next high tide cycle, through 3 PM tomorrow. That's a nuisance-flooding heads-up for low-lying shoreline spots, not a storm.

What would change the call: Nothing realistic in this window — it would take new echoes developing upstream, and the model shows no instability to support that.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction wandering
wind.tactics_blurb: Drifter conditions: 3–4 kt from the east, swinging to a light northerly after dark. Stay center, stay off the Tod's Point shore while it's easterly, and sail toward whatever breeze you can see on the water.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of day it is: A light gradient-wind evening with no sea breeze. A sea breeze needs the land to be clearly warmer than the water; today the air (about 59°F) is actually a touch cooler than the Sound (60°F) — an air–water temperature difference of −1.4°F — so there's no thermal engine at all. What's left is the faint background flow around high pressure, about 3–5 kt.

Right now: Riverside YC reads SE 3 kt (4 kt 10-minute average, gusts to 8), and the APRS stations around the cove are all under 1 kt — the breeze is very thin and patchy. Station directions disagree widely (only 35% agreement), which is typical of a light-air day where local eddies run the show.

Through the window: The model holds a light easterly (E–ESE, 3–4 kt) through sunset at 5:56 PM and into early evening. Around 8 PM the runs disagree — the latest keeps it easterly, the two prior runs flip it north — so expect that hour to be variable. By 9–10 PM all runs agree on a light northerly land breeze around 4 kt as the land cools below the water.

Where the pressure is: In an easterly the Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) peninsula shelters the cove, so the east side of the course will be the lightest; the cove is often near-dead in this direction even when the open Sound has some breeze. Once it goes northerly it blows off the land — puffy and shifty, with the best average pressure mid-cove away from the lee of trees and houses. Neither side is reliably favored, so stay center and keep options open.

What the fleet will feel: 3–4 kt is drifter-class racing — heavier boats will struggle to steer, and a race may not get off or may be shortened. Keep weight forward and to leeward, head for visible ripples rather than committing to a side, and expect a big direction change if racing runs past 8 PM.
